title: Multi-Agent Patterns from Spotify’s AI Powered Advertising Platform
gist: Spotify senior engineer Pratik Rasam details how Spotify Ads Manager runs production multi-agent systems on Google ADK Java: more than 70% of ads use AI tools, with about 20,000 creatives generated for over 7,000 advertisers. The core lessons are one agent/one package/one owner, putting anything deterministic in code, tool schemas as prompt engineering, and tracing-first evaluation.

insights.claim: Since launch last year, more than 70% of Spotify ads use AI tools, with around 20,000 creatives generated for over 7,000 advertisers, and most creative-generation pipelines now run through Spotify Ads AI.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Concrete adoption figures show agentic ad creation is in real production, not a demo.
insights.quote: more than 70% of ads currently are using AI tools
insights.locator: Since we launched last year

insights.claim: Ads AI extracts an advertiser's natural-language brief into intent (audience, geo, goal), feeds it to a Google ADK Java orchestration layer through an LLM gateway on Vertex AI, and runs parallel script-generation, guardrail and (in pilot) audience-recommendation agents.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Reference architecture for agentic ad creation on GCP.
insights.locator: What 'Ads AI' Actually Means

insights.claim: Each agent is one package with one owner, enforced by Bazel visibility at compile time, with ownership metadata (lib-info), a monitoring YAML for dashboards and PagerDuty alerts, and LLM config in front matter, so metrics and alerting exist before any agent instructions are written.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Ownership and observability are built into the platform scaffolding, limiting agent sprawl.
insights.locator: One Agent, One Package, One Owner

insights.claim: Safety and orchestration are enforced in a separate layer rather than inside each agent, to keep common guardrails consistent across the agentic experience, with a shared platform for metrics, tracing and an internal moderation layer.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Centralized guardrails avoid per-agent policy drift.
insights.locator: The AI agents layer is where individual agents actually reside

insights.claim: Multi-agent moved from research demo to architecture in 2026 because three supply-side changes (reliable JSON and schema output, frameworks such as LangChain4j, Google ADK and CrewAI, and OTel GenAI observability conventions) combined with one demand-side change (multi-entry products and closed-loop ad measurement).
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Explains the timing: tooling maturity plus product need.
insights.quote: Until early 2026, multi-agent was a research demo, now it is an architecture.
insights.locator: Multi-agents were always there

insights.claim: Standardized OTel GenAI tracing lets teams replay production traces and judge models without writing synthetic tests, reducing black-box behavior.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Standard telemetry lowers the cost of evaluating agents.
insights.locator: What changed in observability

insights.claim: In the old campaign flow each step (objective, targeting, budget, creative) is isolated, so context dies at the creative step; a shared agent session state accumulates brand tone, audience, locale and past performance to give richer signals than the five leaf inputs used today.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: The multi-agent value is shared context across steps, not just parallelism.
insights.locator: Let's just talk about how a campaign creation process looks like

insights.claim: Feeding ad performance (click-through, completion, conversion) back into the system creates a closed loop that can tune targeting and models on what works.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Closed-loop performance data is the long-term moat for AI ad generation.
insights.locator: This is the slide where we eventually want to go

insights.claim: Spotify's first attempt was one agent with a mammoth instruction covering script generation, guardrails, audience, search, validation and schema; it was brittle and instruction changes caused hallucinated behavior that was hard to isolate.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: A cautionary lesson against monolithic agents.
insights.quote: we started off with one single agent and a mammoth of an instruction
insights.locator: Before we got things right

insights.claim: The decomposition follows team ownership: the audience team owns the audience resolver and the creative team owns script generation and the guardrail agent, with guardrail and generation running in parallel.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Conway's-law-aligned agent boundaries reduce coordination cost.
insights.locator: This is the decomposition we landed on

insights.claim: Whatever can be deterministically coded should be code: if semantic wording or intent changes, use the LLM, but if rules, catalogs or data change, use code that can be unit tested.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: A clear heuristic for splitting agent versus code responsibilities.
insights.quote: whatever can be deterministically coded should always be deterministically coded
insights.locator: When you ask me, should everything be controlled by agents

insights.claim: The audience agent turned 'women 21-plus in Nashville' into an invalid 21 to 99 age range rejected downstream, and 'parents of teen 13 to 17' into the teens as targets; fixes were enumerating the seven supported age brackets and fixing persona handling.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Even latest LLMs produce niche errors that need deterministic validation.
insights.locator: We had a case where one of the inputs

insights.claim: Geo targeting such as 'the South and the Midwest' (13 and 12 states) can resolve Georgia as a country unless the tool receives a country code, which Spotify now passes as tool context.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Passing context via tools is a guardrail against ambiguity.
insights.locator: Another case which is interesting is the geo-targeting

insights.claim: Spotify calls its internal moderation classifier first and returns early on failure before invoking LLMs, because running the guardrail agent regardless of generation wasted tokens; existing non-LLM solutions should gate LLM calls.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Cheap pre-checks cut token spend at scale.
insights.locator: We have an internal moderation classifier

insights.claim: Models are getting better but remain non-deterministic, and the speaker's takeaway is to keep agents small and single-responsibility, since smaller, concise agents perform better.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Applies single-responsibility design to agents.
insights.locator: As a last takeaway, wherever possible

insights.claim: Spotify scaffolded ADK patterns: basic agent with tools, conditional router, sequential pipeline, parallel fan-out/gather and generator-critic loop.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: A reusable pattern vocabulary for agent workflows.
insights.locator: Prototyped Patterns

insights.claim: A single agent with tools has no orchestration overhead and is easy to test, but beyond roughly 8 to 10 tools the LLM may start hallucinating, so split the agent.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Tool count is a practical limit for single agents.
insights.locator: Starting with the basic agent and tools

insights.claim: Sequential pipelines add latency and an upstream failure can poison the whole chain, so independent agents should run in parallel.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Sequencing is a latency and reliability tradeoff.
insights.locator: The next one is a sequential one

insights.claim: A router agent is a single point of failure, adds latency and can over-classify intent when downstream agents overlap, so a backup or default route is needed.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Routing errors silently misdirect all downstream work.
insights.locator: This is an interesting agentic pattern

insights.claim: Parallel agents lack each other's context and consume tokens linearly, and generator-critic loops multiply cost since each iteration is a full LLM round-trip and the critic is also an LLM, so maxIterations is needed to prevent runaway consumption.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Refinement loops need a hard exit to bound token cost.
insights.locator: The last one is more of a refinement approach

insights.claim: Tool schemas and descriptions are sent to the LLM, so tool design is prompt engineering: the schema is the contract that tells the model how to call it.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Underinvested tool descriptions are a common source of agent errors.
insights.quote: Tool design is basically prompt engineering.
insights.locator: Third is tool design

insights.claim: Tools should be tied to agent intent and owned by the owning team rather than being thin wrappers over shared APIs, so two agents can use different tools over the same upstream API.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Agent-specific tools beat generic API wrappers.
insights.locator: If a team owns its agents

insights.claim: Tools should fail gracefully with structured responses that tell the agent what happened, rather than internal server errors, acting as recovery prompts.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Error design determines agent recoverability.
insights.locator: As any other software, tools are subject to failure

insights.claim: Tool calls that compose multiple API calls can aggregate behavior but add latency and cost, since tool calls in a trace also incur LLM calls.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Bundle tools only where it reduces round trips.
insights.locator: Tool delegation has its different patterns

insights.claim: Evaluation that verifies outputs without traces is theater, since traces capture the journey (duration, tool calls, moderation latency, raw input and output) and are a prerequisite for evaluating agents.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Trace everything in production before investing in evals.
insights.quote: If you have an evaluation that just verifies the output without the trace, that's mere theater.
insights.locator: When it comes to evaluation

insights.claim: Spotify uses three evaluation levels: tool trajectory, deterministic assertions (schema, geo IDs, age brackets) and scoped LLM-as-judge for tone, brand fit and coherence, exporting telemetry to OTel/Grafana or Braintrust.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Layered evaluation lowers reliance on expensive judges.
insights.locator: The three levels of evaluation

insights.claim: Live evaluation runs on a configurable sample of production traffic, starting higher for new agents; evaluation is not a merge-build CI gate because it makes LLM calls, but runs offline on demand and in a nightly suite.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Cost-aware eval cadence for LLM systems.
insights.locator: The last thing which I'm going to talk about is live evaluation

insights.claim: A judge is detection, not prevention; each anomaly the judge catches should become a new deterministic assert, so the more asserts exist the less expensive the judge becomes.
insights.speaker: Pratik Rasam
insights.so_what: Ratcheting judge findings into code lowers long-run eval cost.
insights.quote: judge is equal to detection and not prevention
insights.locator: One key thing to identify
